mainTopic: רב's rulings on dangerous cats, three teachings of the sons of רב פפא, and rules for settling ארץ ישראל
overview: This amud opens with the end of a story about רב, שמואל and רב אסי. Each refused to walk in ahead of someone he honored, and the גמרא explains why שמואל was the one who waited. Meanwhile a cat bit off a baby's hand, and רב taught four rules about a dangerous cat: you may kill it, you may not keep it, it has no גזל, and it has no השבת אבידה. The גמרא explains why each rule is needed. It also settles a ברייתא that allows raising cats by saying black cats are harmless and white cats are dangerous, and it traces the cat's parents and grandparents to fit רב's story. Next come three teachings passed down by the sons of רב פפא: sounding the alarm over sores on שבת, a locked door that does not open quickly, and writing a deed for a house in ארץ ישראל on שבת. The גמרא explains each one, and shows that the Rabbis allowed asking a גוי to write the deed for the sake of settling ארץ ישראל. It adds that a buyer of a city must buy roads to it from all four sides. The amud ends by introducing a ברייתא about ten conditions יהושע made when he divided the land, and the list continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Nobody wants to walk in first
steps.stepSummary: שמואל won't go in ahead of רב אסי, and רב אסי won't go in ahead of רב. They decide that שמואל will wait, and רב and רב אסי will go in.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל would not go in before רב אסי, and רב אסי would not go in before רב. They said: Who should stay behind? Let שמואל stay behind, and let רב and רב אסי go in.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: the three rabbis are stuck at the door, because each one is honoring someone else. They solve it by having שמואל wait.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל treats רב אסי as greater than himself, and רב אסי treats רב as his teacher. That creates a chain of respect where nobody can move. The solution is to have שמואל step back, so the order becomes רב, then רב אסי, and שמואל enters after them.

keyTerms.meaning: let him stay behind, let him hold back

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמוּאֵל לָא עָיֵיל קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב אַסִּי,
phrases.english: Shmuel would not go in before Rav Asi,

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַסִּי לָא עָיֵיל קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב.
phrases.english: Rav Asi would not go in before Rav.
They said: Who should stay behind?
Let Shmuel stay behind,
and let Rav and Rav Asi come in.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוּאֵל לָא עָיֵיל קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story that began before this part of the daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since each rabbi defers to a greater one, שמואל waits, and רב and רב אסי enter first.

steps.title: Why not have רב or רב אסי wait instead?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the decision: why was שמואל chosen to stay behind, and not רב or רב אסי?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let רב or רב אסי stay behind!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the decision from the story. Why should שמואל be the one to wait?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the story רב had shown deference to שמואל, so it seems רב treats שמואל as greater. If so, it would make more sense for רב, or רב אסי, to hold back. The גמרא wants to know why the story did not go that way.

phrases.english: But let Rav or Rav Asi stay behind!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the decision made in step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice that שמואל should be the one to stay behind
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב had treated שמואל as greater, so it seems רב or רב אסי should be the one to hold back, not שמואל.

steps.title: רב's respect for שמואל was only a gesture
steps.stepSummary: רב did not really consider שמואל greater. He honored שמואל only because he had once cursed him, so in truth רב ranks first.
steps.simpleTranslation: As for רב, it was just a gesture he did for שמואל. Because of that incident where he cursed him, רב took it upon himself to show שמואל respect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רב's deference to שמואל was not a real statement about who is greater.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed that רב truly saw שמואל as greater. The answer is that רב was only making up for having once cursed שמואל, so this honor was a personal kindness and not a real ranking. In the real order of greatness רב comes first, so it was right for שמואל to wait.

keyTerms.meaning: just a gesture, a mere matter
he took upon himself, he led himself

phrases.english: Rav — it was a mere gesture
that he did for Shmuel;
phrases.notes: That's רב's earlier move of letting שמואל go first.

phrases.english: because of that incident in which he cursed him,
phrases.notes: This points back to a known story where רב once cursed שמואל.

phrases.english: Rav took it upon himself to defer to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב – מִילְּתָא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא דַּעֲבַד לֵיהּ לִשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets רב's earlier behavior as a personal gesture rather than a real ranking
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב truly considered שמואל greater than himself, so רב should have waited.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב only honored שמואל to make up for cursing him. In truth רב ranks highest, so שמואל waits.

steps.title: A cat bites off a baby's hand
steps.stepSummary: While the rabbis were sorting out who goes first, a cat came and bit off a baby's hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile, a cat came and bit off the baby's hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The story suddenly turns to a tragedy that happens during all this. It sets up רב's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This event is what leads רב to teach about cats. It shows that a cat can be truly dangerous, especially to small children. The rulings that follow come straight out of this real case.

keyTerms.meaning: in the meantime, while this was going on

phrases.english: In the meantime,
a cat came
and severed the baby's hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves the story from the seating question to a new event
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A cat injured a baby, which leads to רב's rulings about cats.

steps.title: רב's four rules about a cat
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches publicly: a cat may be killed, may not be kept, is not covered by גזל, and is not covered by השבת אבידה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב went out and taught: A cat — you are allowed to kill it, you are forbidden to keep it, taking it is not counted as stealing, and you do not have to return it to its owner if it gets lost.
steps.whatsHappening: רב responds to the attack by giving a public ruling with four rules about cats.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because a cat can be so dangerous, רב treats it as something harmful rather than as valuable property. So you may kill it, you may not keep it, and the usual property rules of גזל and השבת אבידה do not protect it. Each rule takes away a different kind of protection the owner would normally have.

keyTerms.meaning: taught publicly, gave a public lecture
to keep it, to maintain it

steps.whyThisMatters: These four rules show how הלכה treats a dangerous animal: the danger outweighs the owner's normal property rights.

phrases.english: Rav went out and taught:
A cat — it is permitted to kill it,
and it is forbidden to keep it,
and it is not subject to the prohibition of theft,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין בּוֹ מִשּׁוּם הָשֵׁב אֲבֵידָה לַבְּעָלִים.
phrases.english: and it is not subject to returning a lost item to its owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב's ruling in response to the incident in step 4
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A cat may be killed, may not be kept, is not protected by גזל, and does not need to be returned as an אבידה.

steps.title: Why say both 'may kill' and 'may not keep'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if a cat may be killed, isn't it obvious that it may not be kept? Why does רב need to say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: Since you said 'it is permitted to kill it,' what does 'it is forbidden to keep it' add?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's wording, because the second rule seems to repeat what the first rule already says.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a cat is so dangerous that you may kill it, it seems obvious you should not keep it. So the rule 'אסור לקיימו' looks unnecessary. The גמרא wants to know what new point it teaches.

phrases.english: And since you said 'it is permitted to kill it,'
what is the point of adding 'it is forbidden to keep it'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רב's ruling in step 5
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Permission to kill a cat already implies that you should not keep it, so the second rule seems to add nothing.

steps.title: Keeping a cat is a real איסור
steps.stepSummary: Without the second rule, one might think killing a cat is only allowed but keeping it is fine. רב teaches that keeping it is actually forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: it is permitted to kill it, but there is no איסור in keeping it. So רב teaches us that keeping it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the second rule teaches something new. Keeping a dangerous cat is an actual איסור, not just a choice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מותר להורגו' only gives permission. It does not by itself forbid anything. 'אסור לקיימו' adds that a person who keeps the cat is actively doing something forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: he teaches us (that it is not so)

steps.whatToRemember: רב's four rules about a dangerous cat each say something separate. 'You may kill it' is a permission, and 'you may not keep it' is a real איסור.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think 'allowed to kill' means 'must not keep.' Being allowed to do something is not the same as being required to do it, which is exactly why רב states both rules.

phrases.english: You might have said:
it is permitted to kill it, but there is no prohibition in keeping it;
so he teaches us that keeping it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא, showing that the extra rule prevents a mistaken assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Killing a cat is allowed, but keeping it carries no איסור.
steps.terutzMaskana: Keeping a dangerous cat is an actual איסור.

steps.title: Why say there is no returning a lost cat?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if a cat is not covered by גזל, why must רב add that it is not covered by השבת אבידה?
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: Since you already said a cat is not covered by the law of stealing, why say again that it is not covered by the מצוה of returning a lost item to its owner?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's list again, this time asking about his last rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you are even allowed to take a cat from its owner, because there is no גזל, then you surely don't have to return one you find. So the rule about השבת אבידה seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it further? (why add this?)

phrases.english: They say: And since you said
"it is not subject to the law of theft,"
what is the point of saying further
"it is not subject to returning a lost item to its owner"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same kind of question as Step 6, now aimed at the last two rules on רב's list.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that a cat is not covered by השבת אבידה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Having no גזל should already mean there is no duty to return it, so the extra rule seems pointless.

steps.title: The rule is about the cat's hide
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that the השבת אבידה rule refers to the cat's hide.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: It refers to its hide.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא explains what the extra rule is really talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule does not just repeat the rule about גזל. It teaches something about the cat's skin. Even the hide, which has value, does not have to be returned to the owner.

phrases.english: Ravina said: To its hide.
phrases.notes: "Its" is the cat: רב's last rule is talking about the cat's skin, not the live cat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the rule a different subject: the hide rather than the live cat.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The השבת אבידה rule just repeats what we already know from the rule about גזל.
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches that even the cat's hide need not be returned.

steps.title: A ברייתא says you may raise cats
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב from רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, who allows raising cats and similar animals because they clean the house of pests.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says one may raise village dogs, cats, monkeys and genets, because they keep the house clean of pests.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to clash with רב's rule that one may not keep a cat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said keeping a cat is forbidden. Here a תנא openly allows raising cats because they are useful. That looks like a direct contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: To clean out the house (of mice and pests)

phrases.aramaic: מֵיתִיבִי, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: They raised an objection: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
One may raise village dogs,
and cats, and monkeys, and genets,
phrases.notes: A genet is a small wild cat-like animal that hunts mice.

phrases.english: because they serve to clean the house!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge against רב's rule that one may not keep a cat.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that keeping a cat is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא explicitly permits raising cats.

steps.title: Black cats versus white cats
steps.stepSummary: No contradiction: the ברייתא is about black cats, and רב is about white cats.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is about a black cat, and that one is about a white cat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the clash by saying the two sources talk about different kinds of cats.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Black cats are harmless, so the ברייתא allows raising them. White cats are dangerous, so רב forbids keeping them.

phrases.english: It is not difficult;
this is with a black one, that is with a white one.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא's permission is for a black cat. רב's ban is for a white cat, which is the dangerous kind.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא; הָא בְּאוּכָּמָא, הָא בְּחִיוּוֹרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases: each source is about a different type of cat.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב and the ברייתא disagree about keeping cats.
steps.terutzMaskana: Black cats may be raised; white cats may not.

steps.title: But רב's cat was black
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the cat in רב's story was black, yet it was dangerous.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the cat in רב's story was black!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the black-versus-white answer against the story that started רב's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cat that bit off the baby's hand was black. So black cats can be dangerous too, and the answer of Step 11 seems to fail.

phrases.english: But the incident of Rav, it was a black one!
phrases.notes: This is the cat from Step 4 that bit off the baby's hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that only white cats are dangerous
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The dangerous cat in רב's story was black.

steps.title: A black cat born to a white cat
steps.stepSummary: The cat in רב's story was black, but its parent was white, so it was dangerous.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it was a black cat that was the offspring of a white cat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why that black cat was still dangerous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cat's parent matters, not only its color. A black cat born to a white cat counts as the dangerous kind.

phrases.english: There, it was a black one, son of a white one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case: the black cat had a white parent.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A black cat is always harmless.
steps.terutzMaskana: A black cat born to a white cat is dangerous.

steps.title: But רבינא was unsure about this case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: רבינא asked about a black cat born to a white cat and left it unsure, so how can we say for certain it is dangerous?
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבינא raised this very case as an open question! For רבינא asked: What is the law of a black cat that is the offspring of a white cat?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of Step 13 by pointing to a question רבינא asked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 treated a black cat with a white parent as definitely dangerous. רבינא, however, asked about exactly that case without knowing the answer. So it cannot be a settled fact.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked it as an open question

phrases.english: But Ravina asked about it as an open question!
For Ravina asked:
A black one, son of a white one, what is it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a black cat born to a white cat is definitely dangerous
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבינא treated that exact case as an unanswered question.

steps.title: Going back one more generation
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asked about a black cat whose white parent came from a black grandparent. רב's cat had a white parent and a white grandparent, so it was surely dangerous.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבינא was unsure, it was about a black cat, offspring of a white cat, which was itself the offspring of a black cat. The cat in רב's story was black, offspring of a white cat, which was itself the offspring of a white cat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by showing that רבינא's case and רב's case had different grandparents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא's doubt was about a mixed family line: black, then white, then black. רב's cat came from two white generations, so its dangerous nature is clear. That way there is no clash, and רב's ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Offspring of a white cat that was itself from a white cat

steps.whatToRemember: רב forbids keeping a dangerous cat. A white cat is dangerous. A black cat whose parent and grandparent were white is dangerous too. רבינא was unsure only about a black cat whose white parent came from a black cat. Black cats in general may be raised, as the ברייתא says.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two family lines. רבינא's case ends with a black grandparent, and רב's case ends with a white grandparent. That one difference settles the question.

phrases.english: When Ravina was asking his question,
it was about a black one, son of a white one, son of a black one;
the incident of Rav

phrases.aramaic: בְּאוּכָּמָא בַּר חִיוָּרָא בַּר חִיוָּרָא הֲוָה.
phrases.english: was with a black one, son of a white one, son of a white one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of Step 14 and closes the black-versus-white discussion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases by tracing the cat's family back another generation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבינא's question and the story of רב are about the same kind of cat.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבינא was unsure about black, then white, then black. רב's cat was black, then white, then white, which is clearly dangerous.

steps.title: Three teachings passed down through the sons of רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: A memory aid and a chain of names (in three versions) introduce three teachings: we sound the alarm on שבת over sores, a locked door does not open quickly, and we may write a deed for buying a house in ארץ ישראל even on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: (A memory aid for the names.) רבי אחא בר פפא said in the name of רבי אבא בר פפא, in the name of רבי אדא בר פפא. Some say רבי אבא בר פפא said it in the name of רבי חייא בר פפא, in the name of רבי אחא בר פפא. And some say רבי אבא בר פפא said it in the name of רבי אחא בר פפא, in the name of רבי חנינא בר פפא: We sound the alarm over an outbreak of sores on שבת. A door that is locked will not be opened quickly. And when someone buys a house in ארץ ישראל, we write the deed for him even on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It lists who passed down three teachings, gives three versions of the chain of names, and then states the three teachings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The memory aid helps you keep the brothers' names straight, because they all end in בר פפא and differ only in their first names. The first teaching, sounding the alarm over sores on שבת, is the one the גמרא will question next. The other two teachings are explained later, in Steps 20 and 25.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid, here for the names in the list
We sound the alarm (a public outcry and prayer in a time of danger)
An itchy skin disease that spreads among people, sores
His deed of purchase, the bill of sale

steps.confusionAlert: Don't get lost in the names. All three versions agree on the three teachings. They only disagree about which brothers passed them on.

phrases.english: (Ḥet-beit-dalet, beit-yod-ḥet, beit-ḥet-nun: a memory aid.)
Rabbi Aḥa bar Pappa said
in the name of Rabbi Abba bar Pappa
in the name of Rabbi Adda bar Pappa,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר פָּפָּא
phrases.english: and some say: Rabbi Abba bar Pappa said
in the name of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Pappa
in the name of Rabbi Aḥa bar Pappa,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר פָּפָּא
phrases.english: and some say: Rabbi Abba bar Pappa said
in the name of Rabbi Aḥa bar Pappa
in the name of Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa:
We sound the alarm over an outbreak of sores on Shabbat,
and a door that is locked will not be opened quickly,
and one who buys a house in Eretz Yisrael,
we write his deed for it even on Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא בַּר פָּפָּא מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the discussion of cats that ended in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We sound the alarm over sores on שבת; a locked door does not open quickly; a deed for buying a house in ארץ ישראל may be written even on שבת.

steps.title: A ברייתא says we do not sound the alarm over sores
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects from a ברייתא that lists sores among troubles for which we do not sound the alarm, but only cry out.
steps.simpleTranslation: They objected: For other troubles that break out on the community, such as sores, locusts, flies, hornets, mosquitoes, or an attack of snakes and scorpions, they would not sound the alarm. Instead they would cry out!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first teaching from step 16. It quotes a ברייתא that clearly says we do not sound the alarm over sores.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 16 said we sound the alarm over חיכוך on שבת. The ברייתא names חיכוך directly as a case where we do not sound the alarm, only cry out. The two sources seem to contradict each other head-on.

keyTerms.meaning: Cry out (in prayer), a lesser response than sounding the alarm

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
And other calamities
that break out and come upon the community,
such as sores, locusts, flies,
hornets, and mosquitoes,
and an attack of snakes and scorpions,
they would not sound the alarm, but would cry out!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the first teaching of step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The teaching that we sound the alarm over sores on שבת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא names sores directly as a case where we only cry out and do not sound the alarm, which is a direct contradiction.

steps.title: Moist sores versus dry sores
steps.stepSummary: No contradiction: one source is talking about moist sores and the other about dry sores.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here it is talking about moist sores, and there it is talking about dry sores.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two sources are talking about two different kinds of sores.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sores can be moist or dry. The teaching that we sound the alarm on שבת is about moist sores. The ברייתא, which says we only cry out, is about dry sores.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction

phrases.english: It is not difficult;
here it is about moist sores, there it is about dry sores.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא; כָּאן בְּלַח, כָּאן בְּיָבֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source is about a different kind of sore.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to be about the same sores, so they contradicted each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: For the dangerous dry sores we sound the alarm even on שבת; for moist sores we only cry out.

steps.title: Proof that sores can be moist or dry
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that the boils of מצרים were moist outside and dry inside, which shows that sores come in both forms.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יהושע בן לוי said: The boils that הקדוש ברוך הוא brought on the Egyptians were moist on the outside and dry on the inside, as it says: "And it became a boil with blisters breaking out on man and on beast."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports its answer by showing from a פסוק that sores really can be moist or dry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "breaking out" with blisters show that the outside of the boil oozed. Since the פסוק describes only the outside as wet, we learn that the inside was dry. So the split between moist and dry sores in step 18 is a real distinction, not one made up just to answer the question.

keyTerms.meaning: Boils, the skin plague of מצרים
Breaking out, spreading on the skin

steps.whatToRemember: We sound the alarm on שבת over moist sores. For dry sores we only cry out, as the ברייתא says. The boils of מצרים show that both kinds exist.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁחִין שֶׁהֵבִיא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עַל הַמִּצְרִים –
phrases.english: The boils that the Holy One, Blessed be He, brought upon the Egyptians
were moist on the outside and dry on the inside,
as it says:
"And it became a boil with blisters
breaking out upon man and upon beast."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to back up the moist/dry split of step 18.
steps.raayaObject: That sores really come in moist and dry forms.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהושע בן לוי's reading of the פסוק about the boils in מצרים (שמות 9:10).

steps.title: What does the locked door mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the second teaching from Step 16, 'a locked door will not open quickly,' and asks what it refers to.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And a door that is locked will not be opened quickly': what is this talking about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the second of the three teachings and asks what it means. This sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase is clearly not about a real door; it is a saying with a deeper message. The גמרא wants to know what situation the saying is describing.

keyTerms.meaning: A door that is locked (a saying, not a real door)
What is it? (asking what something means)

phrases.english: "And a door that is locked
will not be opened quickly": what is it?
phrases.notes: This is the second of the three teachings from the memory aid in Step 16.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After resolving the first teaching about sores (Steps 17-19), the גמרא moves on to the second teaching.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the saying about a locked door refers to.

steps.title: מר זוטרא: it means ordination
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא explains that the locked door refers to סמיכה (rabbinic ordination).
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said: It refers to ordination.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא gives the first answer: the saying is about receiving סמיכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone tries to get סמיכה and the door is shut on him, that chance will not open up again soon.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra said: Ordination.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The locked door refers to סמיכה.

steps.title: רב אשי: bad luck doesn't turn quickly
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the saying means anyone who is treated badly will not soon be treated well.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Anyone who is treated badly will not soon be treated well.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a second, more general answer: the locked door is about a person's bad fortune.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike מר זוטרא, who limits the saying to סמיכה, רב אשי reads it as a general rule of life. Once things go badly for someone, good does not return quickly.

keyTerms.meaning: They treat him badly; things go badly for him
They treat him well; things go well for him

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Anyone who is treated badly
will not quickly be treated well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different explanation from מר זוטרא's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The saying is about a person who suffers misfortune: good will not come back soon.

steps.title: רב אחא מדיפתי: good never returns
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדיפתי goes further than רב אשי and says such a person will never be treated well.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא מדיפתי said: He will never be treated well.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא מדיפתי gives a harsher version of רב אשי's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said good comes back slowly. רב אחא מדיפתי says it never comes back at all.

phrases.english: Rav Aḥa of Difti said:
He is never treated well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רב אשי's reading but makes it stronger.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A person who suffers misfortune never sees good again.

steps.title: רב אחא's view was only personal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רב אחא מדיפתי's view and says he was only describing his own experience.
steps.simpleTranslation: But that is not so. רב אחא מדיפתי was saying something that reflected his own life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets aside רב אחא מדיפתי's harsh view and says it is not a true general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His statement came from his own bad experience, not from a principle that applies to everyone. That leaves רב אשי's gentler reading in place: good returns, just not quickly.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is not so (rejecting a view)
A matter about himself; his own situation

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not rejecting the whole idea of the locked door. It only rejects the word 'never'.

phrases.english: But it is not so;
Rav Aḥa of Difti
was saying a matter about himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the view of Step 23.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only רב אחא מדיפתי's claim that good never returns.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: His view reflects his own experience, not a general truth.

steps.title: Writing a deed on שבת?!
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the third teaching, that a deed for a house in ארץ ישראל may be written even on שבת, and objects: how can anyone write on שבת?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And one who buys a house in ארץ ישראל, we write the deed for him even on שבת.' On שבת? Can that really be what it means?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the third teaching and immediately challenges it. Writing is a forbidden מלאכה on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Writing is one of the core forbidden labors of שבת, so a Jew cannot write a deed then. The question sets up the explanation that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: His deed; the document of sale
Would it enter your mind? (meaning: surely not)

phrases.english: And one who buys a house in Eretz Yisrael:
we write his deed of sale for him
even on Shabbat.
On Shabbat? Would that enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the third teaching from Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The teaching that a deed for a house in ארץ ישראל may be written on שבת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Writing is a forbidden מלאכה on שבת, so it cannot be allowed.

steps.title: A גוי writes it, and the Rabbis allowed this
steps.stepSummary: Following רבא, the גמרא explains that a Jew tells a גוי to write the deed. Asking a גוי is normally forbidden by the Rabbis, but they did not forbid it here because of settling ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is like רבא said elsewhere: he tells a גוי, and the גוי does it. Here too, he tells a גוי and the גוי writes it. Asking a גוי is normally a rabbinic prohibition, but the Rabbis did not apply it here because of settling ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: the Jew does not write the deed himself. He asks a גוי to write it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Telling a גוי to do a forbidden labor for you is normally a שבות, a rabbinic prohibition. The Rabbis chose not to apply this ban here, because settling ארץ ישראל is so important.

keyTerms.meaning: Telling a non-Jew to do a forbidden labor on שבת

steps.whatToRemember: A Jew may ask a גוי to write a deed for a house in ארץ ישראל on שבת. The usual rabbinic ban was lifted for the sake of יישוב ארץ ישראל.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the Rabbis could set aside one of their own decrees for the sake of a great מצוה like settling ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: Rather, as Rava said there:
He tells a gentile, and he does it;
here too, he tells a gentile, and he does it.
And even though telling a gentile
is a rabbinic prohibition,
because of settling Eretz Yisrael
the Rabbis did not decree regarding it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the writing is done by a גוי, not by the Jew.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It sounded as if a Jew himself writes the deed on שבת.
steps.terutzMaskana: A גוי writes it at a Jew's request. The usual rabbinic ban on this was not applied, for the sake of settling ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: Buying a city: roads on all four sides
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן teaches that someone who buys a city in ארץ ישראל is forced to buy roads to it from all four sides, for the sake of settling the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: One who buys a city in ארץ ישראל is forced to buy a road to it from all four of its sides, because of settling ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a related teaching that also rests on the value of settling ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer is not left to decide for himself. בית דין forces him to buy roads from every side, so the city can be reached and lived in.

keyTerms.meaning: We force him (בית דין compels him)

steps.whatToRemember: Settling ארץ ישראל is important enough to lift a rabbinic ban on שבת and even to force a city's buyer to make it reachable from every side.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
One who buys a city in Eretz Yisrael:
we force him to buy a road to it
from its four sides,
because of settling Eretz Yisrael.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another rule based on the same value of יישוב ארץ ישראל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A buyer of a city in ארץ ישראל is forced to buy roads to it from all four sides, because of יישוב ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: Introducing the ten conditions of יהושע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says יהושע made ten conditions when he divided ארץ ישראל. This line introduces the list that comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught in a ברייתא: יהושע made ten conditions.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new ברייתא that says יהושע set ten conditions. This line is a setup: the ten conditions will be listed in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The steps before this one were about special rules made for the sake of settling ארץ ישראל. This ברייתא adds a source from the time of יהושע. When he gave the land to the tribes, he attached conditions that every owner had to accept.

keyTerms.meaning: יהושע, who led the Jews into ארץ ישראל and divided it among the tribes

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not list the conditions yet. It only tells you that a list of ten is coming.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Joshua stipulated ten conditions:

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן, עֲשָׂרָה תְּנָאִין הִתְנָה יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבי יונתן's rule about roads for settling ארץ ישראל, the גמרא brings a related ברייתא about conditions that יהושע made when dividing the land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יהושע set ten conditions on the land when he divided ארץ ישראל among the tribes. The list follows.
